procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Bombay at Aurangabad
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 23.01.2020 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay at Aurangabad in CRLA No. 859 of 2019
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The son of the appellants (former husband of the complainant) filed proceedings before the High Court to quash criminal proceedings u/ss.498-A, 312, 313 and 34 of the Penal Code, 1860. The High Court did not exercise its inherent powers u/s.482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the criminal proceedings.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, aggrieved by the High Court's decision, filed the present appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 5542 of 2024) in the Supreme Court. Notice was issued by the Supreme Court on 2nd June 2020. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal. A separate Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No. 3298 of 2020 was filed by the son of the appellants, but it was disposed of as abated due to his death on 10th December 2024.

directions: The impugned judgment and order dated 23rd January 2020 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay at Aurangabad in Criminal Application No. 859 of 2019 is quashed and set aside;

The criminal proceedings against the appellants in FIR No. 339 of 2018 and Final Report No. 10 of 2021 on the file of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Latur and all subsequent proceedings arising therefrom are quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court should have exercised its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the criminal proceedings against the appellants.

facts: A complainant filed an FIR against her parents-in-law (the appellants) under Sections 498-A (cruelty), 312 (causing miscarriage), and 313 (causing miscarriage without woman's consent) of the IPC.
The FIR alleged that the appellants gave the complainant poisonous food, which led to a miscarriage.
The appellants filed an application in the High Court under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the FIR, but the High Court dismissed it.

The Supreme Court noted several inconsistencies: the complainant lived in a separate house from the appellants, and there was no mention in the FIR that she had ever informed the appellants or her husband about the pregnancy.
Furthermore, the criminal complaint was filed only after the complainant had sent a notice for divorce, and this prior divorce notice contained no allegations of cruelty or miscarriage.
law: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), a High Court has inherent powers to quash criminal proceedings to prevent an abuse of the process of law.

Citing the precedent in *State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal*, the Court reiterated the principle that proceedings can be quashed if the allegations in the FIR, even if taken at face value, do not prima facie constitute a case against the accused.
application: The Court analyzed the facts and found the allegations to be suspect. It considered it highly "unusual" that an FIR alleging the appellants caused a miscarriage would completely omit the crucial fact of whether the appellants even knew about the pregnancy.

The Court also found the timing of the complaint to be significant. The fact that these serious allegations were made only after a divorce notice was sent, and were absent from the notice itself, suggested an "ulterior motive."

The Court concluded that the criminal proceedings were likely initiated to pressure the appellants' son into consenting to a divorce on the complainant's terms and were being used as a "weapon" in a personal dispute.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that allowing the criminal proceedings to continue against the appellants would be an abuse of the process of law. Therefore, it held that this was a fit case where the High Court should have exercised its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the proceedings. The Supreme Court then quashed the FIR and all related proceedings against the appellants.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court should have exercised its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the criminal proceedings against the appellants.
appellant_arguments: The criminal complaint was a pressure tactic, and the appellants and their son did not succumb to it.
respondent_arguments: The respondent-complainant supported the contentions of the respondent-state, arguing against the quashing of the criminal proceedings. (The text does not specify the detailed arguments made by the respondents).

cases.case_name: State of Haryana and Others v. Bhajan Lal and Others
cases.principle: For the illustrative categories of cases wherein the extraordinary power under Article 226 of the Constitution or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure could be exercised to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. Specifically cited for the categories where: (1) the allegations in the FIR do not disclose a cognizable offence, and (2) there is an express legal bar to the institution and continuance of the proceedings.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The continuance of criminal proceedings that result in an abuse of the process of law must be quashed by the High Court in the exercise of its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
obiter: The High Court can exercise its power to quash proceedings where there is an express legal bar to the institution and continuance of the proceedings under the relevant Code or Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The continuance of the criminal proceedings against the appellants would result in an abuse of process of law, and therefore, it was a fit case for the High Court to have exercised its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the proceedings.
legal_tests_applied:
The court applied the categories of cases laid down in State of Haryana and Ors. v. Bhajan Lal and Ors. (1992 Supp. 1 SCC 335) where the extraordinary power under Article 226 or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code could be exercised to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. The specific categories cited were:
1. Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused.
2. Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.
3. Where there is an express legal bar engrafted in any of the provisions of the Code or the Act concerned to the institution and continuance of the proceedings.
4. Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fides and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge.
policy_considerations: The inherent powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. should be exercised to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.
